specPoints.text: practical: obtain a temperature–time graph to show the constant temperature during a change of state

primer.text: This practical watches ice become water on a temperature–time graph and catches the melting plateau red-handed: while the change of state runs, the thermometer refuses to move. The method, the expected flat region, and the honest error analysis are all part of the mark scheme.

lessons.title: Aim and equipment of the melting-ice practical
lessons.opening: The investigation has one target: record how the temperature of crushed ice behaves as it is heated steadily, and reveal the plateau at the melting point. The kit list is deliberately ordinary so the plateau is not hidden by apparatus quirks.
keyPoints: The aim is to obtain a temperature–time graph showing constant temperature while ice melts.
Crushed ice is used so the thermometer bulb makes good thermal contact throughout the sample.
A thermometer, a beaker, a heat source and a stopwatch form the core equipment set.
Readings are taken at regular, equal intervals of time so the graph is fair.

low.restatement: Melt some crushed ice with a gentle flame, note the temperature every half-minute, and plot temperature against time. The graph should climb, sit flat at zero degrees while the ice melts, then climb again.
low.analogy: Filming a staircase where one step is a landing: the temperature climbs, rests on the melting landing for a while, then resumes climbing.
low.examPointer: Quote the aim in the question's own terms — a temperature–time graph showing the constant temperature during the change of state — rather than a vague 'find the melting point'.

medium.restatement: The design manipulates the heating rate (independent variable in time) and measures temperature at fixed intervals, with crushed ice chosen to minimise thermal gradients around the bulb. The plateau is the dependent behaviour of interest: energy supplied during melting is going into the change of state, not into temperature.
medium.analogy: A taxi meter that stops ticking while the passenger changes seats: the engine (heater) keeps running, the fare (temperature) pauses during the transition.
medium.examPointer: If asked why crushed ice rather than a single block, answer thermal contact: small chips surround the bulb so the reading reflects the whole sample, not one warm corner.

check.stem: What is the aim of this practical investigation into melting ice?

options.text: to obtain a temperature–time graph showing constant temperature during melting
options.explanation: The plateau at the melting point is the target evidence.

options.text: to measure the specific heat capacity of ice
options.explanation: That is a different practical; here the plateau itself is the goal.

options.text: to find how fast ice conducts heat
options.explanation: No conduction measurement is made.

options.text: to determine the boiling point of water
options.explanation: The investigation never reaches boiling.

check.stem: Why is crushed ice preferred to a single large block?

options.text: it surrounds the thermometer bulb for better thermal contact
options.explanation: Good contact means the reading represents the whole sample.

options.text: it melts at a lower temperature than block ice
options.explanation: Melting point depends on the substance, not the chunk size.

options.text: it stops the ice from changing state
options.explanation: The change of state is exactly what is being observed.

options.text: it reduces the energy needed to heat the beaker
options.explanation: The beaker's energy cost is unchanged by crushing the ice.

check.stem: Which set of equipment is sufficient for this practical?

options.text: beaker of crushed ice, thermometer, heat source, stopwatch
options.explanation: These four deliver heating, sensing and timed readings.

options.text: voltmeter, ammeter and immersion heater only
options.explanation: Electrical metering belongs to the specific-heat practical, not this one.

options.text: balance and measuring cylinder only
options.explanation: Mass and volume are not measured in this investigation.

options.text: barometer and anemometer
options.explanation: Weather instruments have no role here.

check.stem: Why should temperature readings be taken at equal time intervals?

options.text: equal spacing makes the time axis of the graph even and the plateau clear
options.explanation: Regular sampling yields a fair, evenly scaled temperature–time plot.

options.text: equal spacing lowers the melting point of the ice
options.explanation: Sampling cannot affect the melting point.

options.text: unequal spacing would melt the ice too quickly
options.explanation: Reading frequency does not drive the heating.

options.text: equal spacing is only needed when using a data logger
options.explanation: Regularity matters for manual and logged readings alike.

check.stem: A student proposes measuring the ice temperature once, at the end, after all the ice has melted. Why does this fail the aim?

options.text: a single late reading cannot reveal the plateau during the change of state
options.explanation: The constant-temperature region is only visible from repeated readings across the melt.

options.text: a single reading is always inaccurate
options.explanation: One reading can be accurate; it simply cannot show the plateau.

options.text: the thermometer cannot read liquid water
options.explanation: Thermometers read liquid water perfectly well.

options.text: the ice would not melt without repeated readings
options.explanation: Melting depends on heating, not on reading frequency.

check.stem: State the core equipment needed to obtain the temperature–time graph for melting ice.
check.modelAnswer: A beaker of crushed ice with a thermometer in it, a heat source to warm it steadily, and a stopwatch for timing equal-interval readings.

check.stem: State what is special about the temperature of the ice while it is melting.
check.modelAnswer: While the ice melts its temperature stays constant at the melting point even though heating continues.

check.stem: Explain why the thermometer should sit in the middle of the crushed ice rather than touching the beaker wall.
check.modelAnswer: The beaker wall is heated first and directly by the flame, so glass near the wall can be warmer than the bulk ice. A bulb touching the wall would read the heated glass rather than the sample, exaggerating the temperature and distorting the plateau. Central placement keeps the bulb in thermal contact with the melting ice itself.

check.stem: A class takes readings every 30 seconds for ten minutes. Describe how they should plot the data to meet the aim.
check.modelAnswer: Plot temperature on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis at the 30-second intervals, join the points smoothly, and identify the flat region where the temperature stays constant — that plateau is the melting point during the change of state.

lessons.title: Method and apparatus for the melting-ice practical
lessons.opening: The run itself is a rhythm: heat gently, stir nothing, read on the beat. Gentle heating is the whole trick — too fierce a flame smears the plateau across seconds instead of minutes.
keyPoints: Place the thermometer bulb in the centre of the crushed ice before heating begins.
Heat gently and steadily so the change of state is stretched out in time.
Record the temperature at equal intervals from before melting starts until all the ice has melted.
The apparatus is a beaker of crushed ice over a heat source with the bulb central in the sample.

low.restatement: Bury the bulb in the ice, light a small flame underneath, and take a temperature reading every fixed interval. Keep the flame gentle so the melting stage lasts long enough to be caught by several readings.
low.analogy: Slow-roasting rather than searing: a low heat lets the cook watch every stage of the change instead of skipping past it.
low.examPointer: The words 'gentle' and 'steady' earn method marks — an uncontrolled flame is the classic reason a plateau shows only one reading.

medium.restatement: The apparatus couples a low, steady heating rate to fixed-interval sampling so that the isothermal melt occupies a measurable stretch of the time axis. Starting readings before heating establishes the initial state, and continuing past full melt shows the resumed temperature rise — both anchor the plateau between two climbing limbs.
medium.analogy: A slow-motion replay of a sprint finish: only by slowing the action (gentle heating) can the judge (thermometer) log each frame (reading) of the decisive moment.
medium.examPointer: Describe readings taken before, during and after the melt — the plateau is only convincing if the graph rises, flattens, then rises again.

check.stem: Where should the thermometer bulb be placed before heating starts?

options.text: in the centre of the crushed ice
options.explanation: Central placement samples the bulk of the melting ice.

options.text: resting on the beaker wall
options.explanation: The wall heats first and reads warm.

options.text: held above the ice in the flame's path
options.explanation: The bulb should sense the ice, not the flame.

options.text: outside the beaker for safety
options.explanation: An outside bulb reads nothing useful.

check.stem: Why is gentle heating used in this practical?

options.text: it stretches the melting stage so several readings land on the plateau
options.explanation: A slow melt gives the constant-temperature region enough readings to be visible.

options.text: it raises the melting point of the ice
options.explanation: The melting point is a property of water, not of the flame size.

options.text: it prevents any change of state
options.explanation: The change of state is the observation target.

options.text: it reduces the thermometer's response time to zero
options.explanation: Instruments respond at their own speed regardless of flame size.

check.stem: When should the student stop recording the temperature?

options.text: a few readings after all the ice has melted
options.explanation: Continuing past the melt shows the temperature rising again, framing the plateau.

options.text: as soon as the plateau begins
options.explanation: Stopping at the plateau leaves the second rise unrecorded.

options.text: only after the water boils
options.explanation: Boiling is outside this practical's scope.

options.text: before heating begins
options.explanation: A start-only reading records nothing of the melt.

check.stem: Which sketch matches the expected temperature–time graph for gently heated crushed ice?

options.text: rise, flat region, rise
options.explanation: Warming ice, isothermal melt, warming water — in that order.

options.text: flat region, rise, flat region
options.explanation: Ice starts below the melting point, so the graph does not begin flat.

options.text: a single straight rising line
options.explanation: A straight rise would deny the plateau this practical exists to show.

options.text: a single flat line throughout
options.explanation: Temperature climbs before and after the melt.

check.stem: A student heats strongly and takes readings every 30 seconds, but the plateau shows on only one reading. What went wrong?

options.text: the melt was too fast for the sampling interval — the heating should have been gentler
options.explanation: A fierce flame races through the plateau between readings.

options.text: the thermometer was broken
options.explanation: A working thermometer simply missed the brief plateau.

options.text: the ice was crushed too finely
options.explanation: Fine crushing improves contact; it does not hide plateaus.

options.text: ice has no constant-temperature melt
options.explanation: Melting ice is the textbook isothermal change.

check.stem: State the two heating controls that make the plateau easy to observe.
check.modelAnswer: Heat gently and heat steadily, so the change of state lasts long enough for several equal-interval readings to fall on the plateau.

check.stem: State what the apparatus consists of in this practical.
check.modelAnswer: A beaker of crushed ice standing over a heat source, with a thermometer whose bulb sits centrally in the ice.

check.stem: Explain why the student should record one reading before the heat source is switched on at all.
check.modelAnswer: The pre-heating reading anchors the graph's starting level and proves the ice was below the melting point to begin with. Without it, the initial climbing limb cannot be drawn and the plateau would lack the rise-then-flat structure that identifies the constant-temperature change of state.

check.stem: A class obtains a beautiful plateau but wants to confirm it is the melting point. State the reading they should quote and the two graph features either side of it.
check.modelAnswer: They should quote the flat-region temperature, about 0 °C for ice, bounded by a climbing limb before the melt (solid warming) and a second climbing limb after the melt (liquid warming) — rise, plateau, rise confirms the change of state.

lessons.title: Results and the analysis of the melting curve
lessons.opening: The numbers become a table, the table becomes a curve, and the curve confesses: temperature climbs, refuses to move through the melt, then climbs again. The flat stretch is the energy of change of state made visible.
keyPoints: Readings are tabulated as time against temperature at the fixed sampling interval.
Plotting temperature against time reveals a flat region at the melting point.
The flat region shows energy supplied during melting is not raising the temperature.
After the last ice melts, the temperature of the liquid water rises again.

low.restatement: Write each reading in the table, plot it, and look for the horizontal step. That step sits at zero degrees for melting ice and proves the temperature held constant while the state changed.
low.analogy: A heartbeat trace with a flat pause: the pulse (heating) never stopped, but the trace held its line through the pause.
low.examPointer: When asked to 'use the graph', point at the flat region by name and read its temperature off the axis — that pairing is the analysis mark.

medium.restatement: During the plateau the supplied energy raises the internal energy of the sample by weakening intermolecular attractions rather than by speeding particles up, so the mean kinetic energy — and hence the temperature — is unchanged. The gradient before and after the plateau reflects the specific heat capacities of ice and water respectively, which differ, so the two limbs need not be parallel.
medium.analogy: Paying workers to unbolt seats instead of pushing the rows faster: the money (energy) is spent, the seating chart (state) changes, but the row speed (temperature) pauses.
medium.examPointer: If asked why the two rising limbs have different slopes, answer that ice and water have different specific heat capacities — equal heating raises their temperatures at different rates.

check.stem: What does the flat region of the temperature–time graph represent?

options.text: the change of state at constant temperature
options.explanation: Melting runs isothermally — the flat stretch is the melt.

options.text: a pause in the heating
options.explanation: Heating continued; the energy went into the state change.

options.text: a broken thermometer
options.explanation: The plateau is the expected physics, not an instrument fault.

options.text: the boiling of the melted water
options.explanation: Boiling happens at 100 °C, far beyond this practical.

check.stem: Where does the energy go while the ice is on the plateau?

options.text: into weakening the attractions as the solid becomes liquid
options.explanation: The supplied energy funds the change of state, not the temperature.

options.text: into speeding up the particles
options.explanation: Speeding particles would raise the temperature; the graph shows it constant.

options.text: nowhere — energy flow stops at the melting point
options.explanation: Energy keeps flowing; its effect changes.

options.text: into the beaker only
options.explanation: Some heats the beaker, but the plateau exists because of the ice's change of state.

check.stem: After the last crystal melts, what happens to the graph?

options.text: the temperature rises again as liquid water warms
options.explanation: With no solid left, supplied energy raises the temperature once more.

options.text: the temperature falls back to zero
options.explanation: Nothing cools the sample while heating continues.

options.text: the graph stays flat forever
options.explanation: The flat region ends exactly when the melt ends.

options.text: the graph becomes jagged and unreliable
options.explanation: Nothing about the melt-end introduces noise.

check.stem: Why might the rising limbs before and after the plateau have different gradients?

options.text: ice and water have different specific heat capacities
options.explanation: Different capacities mean the same heating changes their temperatures at different rates.

options.text: the flame was changed mid-practical
options.explanation: With steady heating the flame is not the cause.

options.text: the thermometer drifted out of calibration
options.explanation: Calibration drift would bend the whole curve, not shift one limb's slope.

options.text: the plateau destroys the graph's scale
options.explanation: Axes are unaffected by the shape of the data.

check.stem: A student's graph shows the temperature still climbing slowly through the supposed plateau. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: the sample was unevenly heated, so the bulb region warmed slightly during the melt
options.explanation: Thermal gradients tilt the plateau; stirring-free designs are vulnerable to this.

options.text: ice melts above 0 °C in beakers
options.explanation: The melting point of ice does not care about the beaker.

options.text: the stopwatch was slow
options.explanation: Timing error shifts the axis, not the temperature.

options.text: the graph paper was miscounted
options.explanation: Plotting errors are possible but the systemic tilt points to heating.

check.stem: State what the results table should contain.
check.modelAnswer: Two columns — the time of each reading and the temperature taken at that time, sampled at the fixed equal interval.

check.stem: State the temperature of the flat region for melting ice.
check.modelAnswer: The flat region sits at 0 °C, the melting point of ice.

check.stem: Explain how the graph demonstrates that a change of state occurs at constant temperature.
check.modelAnswer: Between the two rising limbs the plotted line is horizontal: the stopwatch keeps advancing and the heater keeps supplying energy, yet the temperature reading does not change. A temperature that stays fixed while heating continues is only explicable if the energy is being absorbed by the change of state itself, which is exactly what the plateau demonstrates.

check.stem: A class's graph shows a plateau from 2.0 to 6.0 minutes and a pre-plateau gradient twice as steep as the post-plateau gradient. State the melting temperature and describe which phase warms faster per minute under equal heating.
check.modelAnswer: The melting temperature is read from the flat region, about 0 °C, spanning 2.0 to 6.0 minutes. The steeper pre-plateau limb means the solid ice warms faster per minute than the melted water under the same heating, because ice has the lower specific heat capacity.

lessons.title: Evaluating the melt-curve practical and working safely
lessons.opening: No practical is perfect: heat leaks, readings wobble, bulbs touch glass. Naming the systematic and random errors — and the fixes — is as much a part of the practical as the plateau itself.
keyPoints: A systematic error such as heat bypassing the ice tilts or shortens the plateau.
Random reading errors are reduced by averaging and by careful, consistent reading technique.
The main safety duties are handling the hot beaker with tongs or a heatproof mat and keeping the flame controlled.
Eye protection is worn throughout because heated glassware can spit or crack.

low.restatement: Watch out for heat sneaking straight into the thermometer or beaker rather than the ice, and for small wobbly readings. Use goggles, stand the hot beaker on a mat, and lift it with tongs.
low.analogy: Checking a cake recipe: note where heat escaped, accept that every timing jitters a little, and keep the oven gloves on.
low.examPointer: Classify before you fix: systematic errors shift every reading the same way, random errors scatter — improvements should match the error type.

medium.restatement: The dominant systematic threat is energy entering the bulb or glass rather than the sample, which lifts the apparent melt temperature; the control is insulating or repositioning the bulb. Random scatter comes from parallax and reaction-time variation between interval readings; repeating the run and smoothing the plot mitigates it. Safety mirrors any small-scale heating practical: eye protection, heatproof mat, tongs, and flame discipline.
medium.analogy: Calibrating bathroom scales on a tilted floor: no amount of re-weighing (averaging) fixes a tilt (systematic), but the jitter between steps (random) does average out.
medium.examPointer: For the evaluation mark, name the error, name its effect on the plateau, and name the fix — all three, in that order.

check.stem: Which error would shift the whole plateau to a temperature above 0 °C?

options.text: the bulb touching the warmed beaker wall instead of the ice
options.explanation: Reading heated glass systematically inflates the temperature.

options.text: one mistimed reading among many
options.explanation: A single slip is random, not systematic.

options.text: using a stopwatch instead of a data logger
options.explanation: The instrument choice does not bias temperature.

options.text: drawing the axes too small
options.explanation: Presentation does not change measured values.

check.stem: Which improvement reduces random error in the plotted curve?

options.text: repeating the run and plotting a best-fit smoothing through the points
options.explanation: Repetition and smoothing average out scatter.

options.text: replacing the crushed ice with one big block
options.explanation: A block worsens contact and adds systematic error.

options.text: heating more fiercely to finish sooner
options.explanation: Fierce heating hides the plateau entirely.

options.text: reading the thermometer from above at an angle
options.explanation: Parallax adds random error rather than removing it.

check.stem: Why is eye protection required in this practical?

options.text: heated glassware and boiling spits can eject hot material
options.explanation: Goggles guard against splashes and cracking glass.

options.text: ice at 0 °C damages unprotected eyes
options.explanation: The hazard is the heating, not the ice.

options.text: the stopwatch could shatter
options.explanation: Stopwatches are not the hazard here.

options.text: goggles improve reading precision
options.explanation: Goggles protect eyes; they do not change parallax.

check.stem: A plateau is obtained but lasts only two readings. Which evaluation follows?

options.text: reduce the heating rate so the melt spans more readings
options.explanation: A gentler flame stretches the constant-temperature region.

options.text: take fewer readings to shorten the practical
options.explanation: Fewer readings starve the plateau further.

options.text: double the ice but also double the flame
options.explanation: Scaling both leaves the plateau equally brief.

options.text: accept it — plateaus are always one reading long
options.explanation: The plateau duration is under the experimenter's control.

check.stem: A student claims the practical proves 'heat always raises temperature'. Which result contradicts them?

options.text: the plateau, where heating continued but temperature held constant
options.explanation: The flat region is direct counter-evidence during the change of state.

options.text: the first rising limb
options.explanation: That limb supports the claim rather than contradicting it.

options.text: the choice of crushed ice
options.explanation: Equipment choice is not evidence about temperature.

options.text: the safety precautions
options.explanation: Safety is not part of the energy argument.

check.stem: State one systematic error in this practical and its effect on the plateau.
check.modelAnswer: Heat reaching the bulb through the warmed beaker wall is systematic — it raises the apparent melt temperature or tilts the plateau instead of holding it level.

check.stem: State two safety precautions for heating ice in a glass beaker.
check.modelAnswer: Wear eye protection throughout and stand the beaker on a heatproof mat, lifting or moving it only with tongs once hot.

check.stem: Explain why repeating the experiment improves confidence in the plateau but cannot fix a bulb touching the wall.
check.modelAnswer: Repetition averages out random scatter such as reaction-time wobble and parallax, so the plateau's level and duration become more reliable. But a bulb resting on warmed glass biases every run in the same direction — the error is systematic — so repeated runs simply reproduce the inflated value until the placement is corrected.

check.stem: A class must redesign the practical so the plateau spans at least four readings at 30-second intervals. State two changes they should make and the effect each has.
check.modelAnswer: Reduce the flame so the melt lasts longer in time, and start with more crushed ice so there is more solid to melt — together these stretch the constant-temperature region across several 30-second readings, giving at least four points on the plateau.

glossary.definition: A plot of temperature against time used to reveal constant-temperature regions during heating.
The flat region of the graph where temperature stays constant while the state changes.
A repeatable bias that shifts every reading in the same direction.
Unpredictable scatter between readings that averaging can reduce.
